title: H-1B Extension Fees Set To Rise for Large Employers Under Proposed U.S. Rule
excerpt: Companies with heavy H-1B and L-1 workforces may soon pay $4,000-$4,500 per extension petition, a cost that would hit Indian IT firms and their 2.26 lakh extended workers hardest.
body:
• The Trump administration plans to require large employers with over 50% of their U.S. workforce on H-1B or L-1 visas to pay the $4,000-$4,500 "9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee" on extension petitions, not just initial filings
  • Of 4.06 lakh H-1B applications approved in fiscal 2025, nearly 2.9 lakh (71%) were for continued employment — meaning extensions, not new hires, dominate program usage
  • Indians received approximately 2.26 lakh H-1B extensions in fiscal 2025, comprising 77.6% of all extensions globally, making them disproportionately affected by the fee expansion
  • Amazon led with 14,532 approved continuing-employment H-1B applications, followed by TCS (5,293), Microsoft (4,863), Meta (4,740), Apple (4,610), and Google (4,509)

Employers who rely heavily on H-1B and L-1 visa workers may soon face thousands of dollars in additional costs for simply retaining their existing foreign employees, as the Trump administration moves to expand a national security-linked fee to cover visa extensions for the first time.

Regulatory agendas released in early July by the Departments of Homeland Security, Labor, and State signal that a final rule could arrive within weeks. The change would require companies with more than 50 employees in the U.S. — where over half the workforce holds H-1B or L-1 visas — to pay the "9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee" on extension petitions, not just initial filings or employer changes.

The Fee Structure

The fee currently stands at $4,000 per H-1B petition and $4,500 per L-1 petition. Under existing rules, these so-called "50/50 employers" pay the surcharge only when sponsoring a worker for an initial period of stay or when the employee changes employers. Extensions with the same employer have been exempt.

Removing that exemption would hit companies where it hurts most: retention. According to a USCIS report, of the 4.06 lakh H-1B applications approved during fiscal year 2025 (ending September 30), nearly 2.9 lakh — 71% — were for continuing employment rather than first-time entrants. The bulk of program activity involves keeping existing workers, not bringing in new ones.

"The proposed rule would require covered employers to submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension-of-stay petitions, regardless of whether a Fraud Fee applies."

— Department of Homeland Security proposed regulation

Indian Workers Bear the Brunt

The expansion would disproportionately affect Indian nationals, who dominate H-1B extension statistics. Approximately 2.26 lakh Indians received H-1B extensions in fiscal 2025, accounting for 77.6% of the global total of 2.92 lakh extensions. China trailed at 31,581 (10.8%), followed by the Philippines (2,506), Canada (2,186), and South Korea (1,913).

For large IT services firms — the primary targets of the 50/50 threshold — the cumulative cost increase could be substantial. A company extending 1,000 H-1B workers annually would face an additional $4 million in fees. This comes on top of the existing fee structure that already includes base filing fees, fraud prevention fees, and the optional $2,805 premium processing charge.

Who Gets Hit Hardest

Data from the National Foundation for American Policy shows that Amazon had the most approved H-1B applications for continuing employment in fiscal 2025 with 14,532, followed by TCS (5,293), Microsoft (4,863), Meta Platforms (4,740), Apple (4,610), and Google (4,509). The think tank noted these numbers do not represent individual employees, since a single H-1B holder may be approved multiple times in the same year if they change locations.

The fee expansion primarily targets Indian IT outsourcing firms like TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, which typically have the highest ratios of H-1B workers to total U.S. employees. Major U.S. technology companies generally fall below the 50% threshold for their direct hires, though they may face indirect cost increases through their outsourcing contracts.

Legal and Political Context

The proposal has a contested history. A similar attempt to extend the fee to extensions was blocked by a nationwide injunction in 2020. The American Immigration Lawyers Association has challenged the legal basis for the current proposal, arguing it contradicts the "plain language and intent of the statute" that created the fee.

The 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee, established by the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2016, funds national security programs including a biometric entry-exit system to track non-U.S. citizens. DHS argues the expansion is necessary to comply with the congressional mandate to implement that system.

What's Next

The final rule is expected in the coming weeks. For Indian IT professionals and their employers, the practical effect would be to make every three-year extension cycle significantly more expensive. Combined with the $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions — currently blocked by courts — and tightening restrictions on student work authorization, the visa landscape for Indian workers in the U.S. is becoming increasingly costly to navigate.
